# [TITLE C10]

Anonymous authors

Paper under double-blind review

# ABSTRACT

Vision-language models (VLMs) suffer from visual hallucination, such as saying an object that is not present in an image. We ask a more fundamental question: whether a VLM is even aware of where it is looking before understanding the semantic meaning in the image. We formulate this question as a [NAME C10] task: identifying which parts of its visual input were available to the model. We construct the task in a self-supervised way without manually labeling the available region to the model. Our experiments show that existing VLMs fail to localize the visible region. We further show that fine-tuning VLMs on the proposed [NAME C10] task improves a model's awareness of visual input.

# 1 INTRODUCTION

For example, Asadi et al. (2026) show that Gemini-3-Pro, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4.5, and GPT-5.1 can readily produce detailed image descriptions and elaborate re

## 6 RELATED WORK

Visual hallucination. Existing benchmarks such as CHAIR (Rohrbach et al., 2018), POPE (Li et al., 2023), ROPE (Chen et al., 2024b), and HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024) measure different forms of mismatch between visual evidence and generated claims, and methods address such errors through instruction data (Liu et al., 2024a), preference alignment (Sun et al., 2024), or decoding (Leng et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024). Other studies expose limits of visual representations (Tong et al., 2024), elementary perception (Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024), and spatial relations (Kamath et al., 2023). Recently, Asadi et al. (2026) show the illusion even in frontier models where models describe images they were never given. [NAME C10] turns this observation into a quantitative measure, while [NAME C10] targets the underlying capability: knowing what visual input is available before reasoning about what it contains.

## REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT

Sec. 3 specifies the [NAME C10] construction and the positional restoration, Sec. 4 the [NAME C10] construction and scoring, and Sec. 5.1 the training and evaluation protocol. App. A gives the instruction mixture and training recipe, App. E the prompts, and App. F the implementation checks. Accompanying scripts rebuild every table and figure from saved predictions without model inference and record hashes of their inputs.

## ETHICS STATEMENT

The study uses existing research datasets and collects no new human-subject data. Images may depict identifiable people; any release must respect the source datasets' access and licensing terms. Improved awareness of visual input does not guarantee factual or safe outputs, and the models should not be described as having human-like awareness.

We train in bfloat16 using scaled dot-product attention and apply LoRA to all linear layers with rank 16 and α = 32, while keeping the vision encoder and projector frozen. We use a per-device batch size of 1 with 8 gradient-accumulation steps across four GPUs, giving an effective batch size of 32. Training runs for two epochs with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴, a warmup ratio of 0.05, a maximum sequence length of 4096, and a maximum image area of 1,003,520 pixels. We reserve 1% of the combined training examples for validation.

## F VERIFYING THE POSITIONAL RESTORATION

We validate positional restoration independently of downstream performance. Translating the crop patch indices by the grid offset must exactly reproduce the corresponding rows of the full-image position indices. The same row mapping is used to select the absolute interpolation entries, so any indexing error affects both pathways and is detected by this check. We additionally use a painted-patch test to verify the processor's merge-block-major flattening order. After canonical resizing, cropping must leave the retained patch inputs unchanged, and the loader must not upsample the crop. During training, crop offsets must also survive the full dataset-loading pipeline. We therefore log the first active positional-override calls to detect any silent loss of these offsets.

## F VERIFYING THE POSITIONAL RESTORATION

We validate positional restoration independently of downstream performance. Translating the crop patch indices by the grid offset must exactly reproduce the corresponding rows of the full-image position indices. The same row mapping is used to select the absolute interpolation entries, so any indexing error affects both pathways and is detected by this check. We additionally use a painted-patch test to verify the processor's merge-block-major flattening order. After canonical resizing, cropping must leave the retained patch inputs unchanged, and the loader must not upsample the crop. During training, crop offsets must also survive the full dataset-loading pipeline. We therefore log the first active positional-override calls to detect any silent loss of these offsets.

Pegah Khayatan \( ^{1} \)  Jayneel Parekh \( ^{1} \)  Arnaud Dapogny \( ^{1} \)  Mustafa Shukor \( ^{1} \)

## Abstract

Despite impressive progress in capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs), these systems remain vulnerable to hallucinations, i.e., outputs that are not grounded in the visual input. Prior work has attributed hallucinations in LVLMs to factors such as limitations of the vision backbone or the dominance of the language component, yet the relative importance of these factors remains unclear. To resolve this ambiguity, We propose HalluScope, a benchmark to better understand the extent to which different factors induce hallucinations. Our analysis indicates that hallucinations largely stem from excessive reliance on textual priors and background knowledge, especially information introduced through textual instructions. To mitigate hallucinations induced by textual instruction priors, we propose HalluVL-DPO, a framework for fine-tuning off-the-shelf

CHAIR [34], SHR [51], and MMHAL-Bench [38] do not distinguish between hallucinations originating from perception failures, learned object co-occurrence priors, or presuppositions introduced by the instruction itself. As a result, the relative contribution of these factors remains poorly understood, limiting both diagnosis and mitigation.

The model reliably recognizes present objects or the absence of random objects, but tends to hallucinate plausible yet absent (i.e., adversarial) objects, especially when the instruction presupposes their presence. Our HalluVL-DPO framework substantially mitigates this failure mode.

To address this limitation, we introduce HalluScope, a diagnostic benchmark to isolate distinct causes of hallucination in LVLMs. Rather than treating hallucination as a single phenomenon, HalluScope separates errors arising from (i) visual perception limitations, (ii) reliance on learned semantic priors, and (iii) reliance on presuppositions introduced by the instruction. Using this benchmark, we demonstrate that hallucinations in modern LVLMs are predominantly driven by textual instructions, even when visual perception remains

We propose two strategies, Contrastive Hint Augmentation and Post-Hoc Hallucination Injection to address this issue. Additionally, to improve the diversity of hallucinated content in the generated preference pairs we introduce Model-Assisted Answer Inversion.

## 1 Introduction

Large Vision–Language Models (LVLMs) have recently achieved remarkable progress across multimodal tasks such as image captioning, visual reasoning, and instruction following [[20](#bib.bib20), [41](#bib.bib41), [14](#bib.bib14), [42](#bib.bib42), [46](#bib.bib46)]. Despite these advances, they are still prone to visual hallucinations [[38](#bib.bib38), [36](#bib.bib36), [2](#bib.bib2), [12](#bib.bib12)], i.e., generating outputs that are not grounded in the input visual information. Such failures limit the deployment of LVLMs in safety-critical applications such as autonomous systems and medical diagnosis.
While even standalone
visual encoders can exhibit object hallucinations [[24](#bib.bib24), [16](#bib.bib16)],
emerging evidence suggests a different failure mode: even when visual recognition is accurate, modern LVLMs frequently generate incorrect responses, reflecting the dominance of the text modality over the visual modality [[45](#bib.bib45), [15](#bib.bib15), [3](#bib.bib3)]. In such cases, the model’s output is more influenced by the learned object co-occurence priors or the text instruction rather than by the image itself, highlighting the stronger role of language priors in shaping response.

## 4 HalluVL-DPO Framework

In this section, we introduce HalluVL-DPO, a framework for mitigating hallucination failures in LVLMs, particularly those caused by over-reliance on textual instruction presuppositions. Our approach fine-tunes LVLMs using a sample-informativeness based variant of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) [[32](#bib.bib32)], post-training the model to prefer visually grounded responses over hallucinated ones ([Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Weighted Preference Optimization ‣ 4 HalluVL-DPO Framework ‣ When Prompts Override Vision: Prompt-Induced Hallucinations in LVLMs")).
To enable this fine-tuning, we construct a training dataset where each sample is paired with a preferred response and a rejected, hallucinated one. These response pairs provide explicit supervision for learning to favor more grounded outputs. #### C.2.5 Preference Pair Construction.

As described in the main paper, for each sample we construct a preference pair consisting of a chosen and a rejected response.
To generate this contrastive pair, unilateral hint augmentation adds a hint about the presence or absence of objects to the task query.
